p.src: A classical bit has two possible states and nothing between them. We may call them $0$ and $1$, heads and tails, or up and down; the names are labels for two distinct points in a classical state space. A quantum bit also yields two alternatives when measured in a fixed way, but it cannot be described by only two state-space points. The simplest example is the spin of an electron.

u.src: Letting the Classical Picture Fail
en: Letting the Classical Picture Fail

p.src: Begin deliberately with a classical story. Put a tiny magnet in a strong external magnetic field. Unless it is already aligned, it precesses about the field. As it radiates energy, the precession damps and the magnet settles into its lowest-energy orientation. By choosing the direction of the applied field, waiting for this relaxation, and then removing the field, we seem able to prepare the magnetic moment in any desired direction.

p.src: The same apparatus suggests a method of detection. Turn on a field in a chosen direction and observe the radiation produced while the little magnet settles. A classical magnet aligned with the field should emit no energy. One initially opposed to the field should emit the maximum amount, and an intermediate angle should produce an intermediate amount. In that picture the radiated energy varies continuously with the angle.

p.src:
The direction used in preparation has not become irrelevant. It controls the probabilities of the two answers. Prepare the electron up relative to the detector and the up result occurs with certainty. Prepare it down and the transition occurs with certainty. Prepare it horizontally and a vertical detector returns the two answers equally often: $P(\text{up})=\frac12,
  \qquad
  P(\text{down})=\frac12.$ Thus a continuously variable family of preparations leads to a two-valued measurement whose statistics vary continuously.

p.src: Complex Numbers and the Geometry of State Space

u.src: Complex Numbers and the Geometry of State Space
en: Complex Numbers and the Geometry of State Space

p.src:
The required state space is linear: its elements can be added and multiplied by scalars. Its scalars are complex numbers. Write $z=a+ib,
  \qquad
  i^2=-1,
  \qquad
  z^*=a-ib,$ where $a$ and $b$ are real. Complex conjugation produces the positive quantity $\begin{aligned}
  z^*z
  &=(a-ib)(a+ib) \notag\\
  &=a^2+b^2.
  \end{aligned}$ This simple cancellation is the algebraic seed of the probability rule.

p.src:
A complex vector space contains objects $\ket a,\ket b,\ldots$ for which $c\ket a,
  \qquad
  \ket a+\ket b$ are again vectors whenever $c$ is complex. Column vectors give a concrete realization: $\begin{aligned}
    \ket a&=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      a_1\\a_2\\ \vdots\\a_n
    \end{pmatrix},
    &
    c\ket a&=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      ca_1\\ca_2\\ \vdots\\ca_n
    \end{pmatrix},\\[0.7em]
    \ket a+\ket b&=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      a_1+b_1\\a_2+b_2\\ \vdots\\a_n+b_n
    \end{pmatrix}.
  \end{aligned}$ Even the complex numbers themselves form a one-dimensional complex vector space. For an electron spin we shall need two dimensions.

p.src:
To each column ket we associate a conjugate row bra: $\ket a=
  \begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix}
  \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bra a=
  \begin{pmatrix}a_1^*&a_2^*\end{pmatrix}.$ The inner product is then $\braket{b}{a}=b_1^*a_1+b_2^*a_2,$ and the squared norm is $\braket{a}{a}=|a_1|^2+|a_2|^2.$ It is real and nonnegative because every term has the form $z^*z$.

p.src: The detector states are fixed as the two standard basis columns.

p.src:
The coefficients are probability amplitudes. The probability of each detector outcome is the squared magnitude of the corresponding amplitude: $P(+)=|a_+|^2,
  \qquad
  P(-)=|a_-|^2.$ Because these are the only outcomes, $\begin{gathered}
    |a_+|^2+|a_-|^2=1,\\
    \text{or equivalently}\qquad \braket{\psi}{\psi}=1.
  \end{gathered}$ A physical state vector is therefore normalized.

p.src:
Multiplying a state by a complex number of unit magnitude leaves all its probabilities unchanged: $\ket\psi\longmapsto e^{i\phi}\ket\psi,
  \qquad
  |e^{i\phi}a_\pm|^2=|a_\pm|^2.$ Thus two vectors differing only by an overall phase represent the same physical state. A relative phase is different. Replacing only $a_-$ by $-a_-$, for example, cannot generally be removed by multiplying the whole vector by one phase; it can change the results of measurements in another basis.

p.src: Classical Observables and Ensemble Averages

u.src: Classical Observables and Ensemble Averages
en: Classical Observables and Ensemble Averages

p.src:
Having described states, turn to measurable quantities. In a classical system with discrete states $n$, an observable is a real-valued function $f_n$ on those states. If the state is uncertain and described by probabilities $p_n$, its ensemble average is $\langle f\rangle_{\mathrm{ens}}
  =\sum_n p_n f_n.$ The notation does not imply that a single measurement must ever equal this number.

  =\sum_n p_n f_n.$ The notation does not imply that a single measurement must ever equal this number.
en:
Having described states, turn to measurable quantities. In a classical system with discrete states $n$, an observable is a real-valued function $f_n$ on those states. If the state is uncertain and described by probabilities $p_n$, its ensemble average is $\langle f\rangle_{\mathrm{ens}}
  =\sum_n p_n f_n.$ The notation does not imply that a single measurement must ever equal this number.

p.src:
For a coin, assign $f_+=+1$ and $f_-=-1$. Then $\langle f\rangle_{\mathrm{ens}}
  =p_+-p_-.$ A fair coin has average zero. If $p_+=3/4$ and $p_-=1/4$, the average is $1/2$. Neither $0$ nor $1/2$ is an outcome of a single toss; each summarizes many $+1$ and $-1$ results.

p.src:
An especially useful observable is the indicator for one state: $\chi_k(n)=
  \begin{cases}
    1,&n=k,\\
    0,&n\ne k.
  \end{cases}$ Its average is $\langle\chi_k\rangle_{\mathrm{ens}}=p_k.$ Thus knowledge of the averages of all classical observables includes, in particular, knowledge of the probability distribution.

p.src: Matrix action is expanded row by row into the two components of the transformed vector.

u.src: Matrix action is expanded row by row into the two components of the transformed vector.

caption.en: Matrix action is expanded row by row into the two components of the transformed vector.

p.src:
Real two-dimensional vectors make the geometry visible. The matrices $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ respectively stretch every direction uniformly, stretch only the $y$-component, and stretch only the $x$-component. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ interchanges the components and reflects the plane across $x=y$. Meanwhile, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix}v_x\\v_y\end{pmatrix}
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}v_y\\-v_x\end{pmatrix}$ rotates vectors through a clockwise quarter-turn in the convention used at the board. A shear supplies another linear example, although its matrix is left as practice. The essential restriction is linearity: not every imaginable transformation of the plane is represented by a matrix.

p.src: A matrix $M$ is Hermitian when $M_{ij}=M_{ji}^*.$

u.src: A matrix $M$ is Hermitian when $M_{ij}=M_{ji}^*.$
en: A matrix $M$ is Hermitian when $M_{ij}=M_{ji}^*.$

p.src:
The diagonal condition $M_{ii}=M_{ii}^*$ forces every diagonal entry to be real. Off-diagonal entries occur in conjugate pairs. For example, $M=
  \begin{pmatrix}
    r&4+i\\
    4-i&s
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad r,s\in\mathbb R,$ is Hermitian. If all entries happen to be real, Hermitian is the same as symmetric.

p.src: We have reached the minimum language needed for the next step. A qubit is a normalized vector in a two-dimensional complex vector space; amplitudes determine probabilities; and observables are Hermitian matrices. With those pieces in place, spin along arbitrary directions and eventually entangled pairs can be discussed without returning to the classical picture that has already failed.
